item.title: Learning to Decode Concatenated Quantum Codes with Hierarchical Message Passing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Neural-augmented bidirectional message-passing decoding raises the depolarizing pseudo-threshold of the concatenated [[15,7,3]] quantum Hamming code to 12.3%.

Grade 0.473 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Jiahui Wu, Chao Zhang, Zipeng Wu, Shilin Huang

Figure

Block failure rate plotted against physical error probability for concatenation depths L=2 and L=3. Compares the neural message-passing decoder with the bidirectional hard-decision decoder under bit-flip and depolarizing noise.

Asks

Can high-rate concatenated quantum codes be decoded accurately and generically with bounded worst-case latency?

Before

Was 6.5% using a bidirectional hard-decision decoder.

But

Evaluated in numerical simulations under phenomenological and circuit-level depolarizing noise models.

Tools

vector-valued belief propagation · hierarchical decoding graphs · lightweight neural message aggregation · Knill teleportation-based error correction

Abstract

We introduce a neural message-passing framework for decoding general concatenated stabilizer codes. Soft beliefs propagate bidirectionally across concatenation levels, and lightweight neural networks learn only to aggregate incoming messages. For the concatenated [[15,7,3]] quantum Hamming code, the resulting decoder achieves substantially higher thresholds than the state-of-the-art bidirectional hard-decision decoder under both bit-flip and depolarizing noise. In particular, the depolarizing pseudo-threshold nearly doubles, from 6.5% to 12.3%. For many-hypercube codes, a decoder fine-tuned on circuit-level errors in Knill's teleportation-based error correction can achieve lower logical-CNOT failure rates than their dedicated decoder, using a fixed number of message-passing iterations instead of extensive combinatorial search. Our framework provides a generic decoding tool for exploring the design space of concatenated codes, including non-CSS constructions, toward low-overhead fault tolerance.

item.title: Logical Neural Belief Propagation for Linear-Complexity Decoding of Surface Codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — L-NBP attains an error threshold of 17.5% under depolarizing code-capacity noise with linear 𝒪(n) complexity, while matching BP-OSD accuracy at distance d=9 under circuit-level noise using 0.2% of its FLOPs.

Grade 0.460 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Hee-Youl Kwak, Seong-Joon Park, Dae-Young Yun, Eliya Nachmani, Jae-Won Kim

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate across code distances under code-capacity noise, showing the 17.5% threshold for L-NBP, and a comparison of FLOPs versus threshold at d=13 across decoders.

Asks

Can belief propagation decoding on surface codes achieve high logical accuracy and clear threshold behavior while preserving linear complexity?

Before

BP-OSD achieved a threshold of 16.5% at 1.95 M FLOPs (d=13), AMBP achieved 17.0% at 95 M FLOPs, and QECCT achieved 17.1% at 604 M FLOPs under code-capacity noise.

But

Evaluated via numerical simulations on rotated surface codes up to distance d=13 under code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise models.

Tools

Neural belief propagation (NBP) · Logical classifier MLP · End-to-end backpropagation · Continuous soft syndrome extraction

Abstract

Quantum error correction (QEC) requires decoders that achieve high logical accuracy while scaling efficiently with the code length. Belief propagation (BP) is attractive for its linear decoding complexity, but conventional BP decoders often fail to reach sufficient logical accuracy on surface codes. We propose Logical Neural Belief Propagation (L-NBP), a BP-based neural decoder that redirects the decoding objective from physical-level decoding to logical-level decoding. L-NBP first runs a neural BP (NBP) module that produces posterior beliefs, and a logical classifier then transforms these beliefs into a continuous-valued soft syndrome and predicts the logical operator. Because all components in L-NBP are trainable by backpropagation, L-NBP is trained end-to-end, so that the NBP module learns to extract soft syndromes that are favorable for logical classification. On surface codes, L-NBP matches or outperforms the BP with ordered-statistics decoding (BP-OSD) and minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) while retaining the linear complexity of BP, and achieves a threshold of 17.5% under depolarizing noise. Moreover, under circuit-level noise, L-NBP matches the accuracy of BP-OSD on the distance-9 surface code while requiring only 0.2% of its complexity. These results show that combining BP, neural weights, and logical-level decoding enables scalable and high-accuracy quantum decoding.

item.title: High-Throughput Normalized Min-Sum Belief Propagation Decoding for Quantum LDPC Codes with Near-Memory Processing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — DPU-based near-memory processing achieves 1.071×107 decodes/s for normalized Min-Sum BP on the [[144,12,12]] code at p=0.001 with 1 iteration, while keeping serialized X+Z compute latency to 0.873 ms at 5 iterations.

Grade 0.443 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Jeonggeun Seo, Youngsun Han, Leanghok Hour, Dongmin Kim

Figure

Projected decoding throughput versus BP iterations for the 2,560-DPU configuration compared to the 16-logical-CPU baseline at p=0.001.

Asks

Can processing-in-memory architectures provide high throughput and sub-millisecond compute latency for iterative belief-propagation decoding of quantum LDPC codes?

Before

16-logical-CPU baseline achieved 1.22×106 decodes/s under the same conditions (8.8× lower).

But

Simulated kernel execution via uPIMulator under data-qubit Pauli error model with ideal syndrome measurements; excludes host-DPU communication latency.

Tools

DPU-based Processing-in-Memory (UPMEM) · uPIMulator · normalized Min-Sum Belief Propagation · Bivariate Bicycle qLDPC code

Abstract

Real-time quantum error correction requires classical decoders to process growing syndrome workloads with low and predictable latency. For quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, iterative belief propagation (BP) repeatedly updates messages over sparse Tanner graphs, creating substantial memory-access and data-movement demands. We map normalized Min-Sum BP decoding of the [[144,12,12]] Bivariate Bicycle qLDPC code onto a DPU-based Processing-in-Memory (PIM) architecture. Within each DPU, 11 tasklets cooperatively decode one syndrome, while multiple DPUs process independent syndrome instances in parallel. Using uPIMulator and a data-qubit Pauli error model with ideal syndrome measurements, we compare throughput, per-syndrome processing time, logical error rate (LER), and single-syndrome tail latency against a 16-logical-CPU baseline. At a component-wise physical error probability of p=0.001 and one BP iteration, the projected aggregate kernel throughput of 2,560 DPUs reaches 1.071 x 10^7 decodes/s, compared with 1.22 x 10^6 decodes/s for the CPU, an 8.8x improvement. From two iterations onward, the measured LER remains below the physical error probability for every evaluated value of p. For one to five iterations, the maximum sampled serialized X+Z DPU compute latency remains below the 1 ms decoder-side reference for trapped-ion QEC, reaching approximately 0.873 ms at five iterations. These results show that near-memory processing can provide high aggregate throughput and sub-millisecond compute latency for qLDPC BP decoding under the evaluated conditions.

item.title: High-Dimensional Deterministic Secure Quantum Communication with Reed-Solomon Erasure Coding
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Theoretical prepare-and-measure DSQC protocol combines classical Reed-Solomon erasure coding with transverse spatial qudits, yielding intercept-resend error rate EIR=12d−1d across b=2 mutually unbiased bases without quantum memory or entanglement.

Grade 0.421 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance” · L. F. A. de Sousa Moura, G. L. Zanin, P. H. Souto Ribeiro, C. Becker Westphall

Figure

Proposed experimental setup for high-dimensional DSQC using SPDC heralded photon pairs, spatial modulation via SLM or DMD, and time-gated matrix single-photon detection.

Asks

Can high-dimensional qudits and classical erasure coding implement deterministic secure quantum communication resilient to noise without requiring quantum memory?

But

Theoretical design; assumes single-photon heralded states, prime alphabet dimension q, and total photons per block n<q.

Tools

Reed-Solomon erasure coding · Transverse Spatial Degrees of Freedom (TSDF) · Mutually Unbiased Bases (MUB) · Heralded SPDC source · Spatial light modulators (SLM)

Abstract

Deterministic Secure Quantum Communication (DSQC) is a quantum cryptographic technique engineered to transfer a message through a quantum channel, requiring an auxiliary classical channel for eavesdropping verification and decoding, but without prior key distribution. This article presents a theoretical high-dimensional prepare and measure DSQC protocol using the Reed-Solomon erasure coding to ensure data resilience to noise. This protocol offers the following benefits: it eliminates the need for quantum memory or entanglement, it can be built with commercially available technology, and its higher capacity improves the overall transmission rate.

item.title: Error-Adaptive Quasi-local Decoding of the Toric Code
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Quasi-local renormalization-group decoder initialized with target and buffer sizes a0=b0=d/8 achieves a whole-system logical-failure crossing window at physical error rate p×comp≈0.09–0.10.

Grade 0.410 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Hossein Dehghani, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, Michael Gullans

Figure

Logical failure probability versus physical error rate p for code distances d using the composite quasi-local RG decoder with a0=b0=d/8, exhibiting a crossing near p≈0.09–0.10 along with its finite-size scaling collapse.

Asks

How much of the global minimum-weight perfect matching correction inside a target region is determined by syndrome data in a finite surrounding buffer?

Before

Conventional global minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) threshold for the dephased toric code is pcMWPM≈0.103 (Dennis et al. 2002; Wang et al. 2003).

But

Restricted to dephasing noise (pure Z errors) with perfect syndrome measurements on the 2D periodic toric code. Patch sizes scale as O(d) rather than constant depth.

Tools

subregion matching ratio R_match diagnostic · minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) · composite quasi-local renormalization-group (RG) schedule · checkerboard patch parallelization

Abstract

Topological quantum memories need decoders that are both reliable and scalable, but these goals compete: globally informed decoders are accurate near threshold yet expensive, while strictly local rules are fast but can miss long-range structure. Motivated by recent recoverability and mixed-state viewpoints, we make this tradeoff operational for the dephased toric code through a decoder-level local recoverability diagnostic. We compare global MWPM corrections to quasi-local corrections inside a target region and define a matching ratio R_match, with mismatch ε_match=1-R_match. Across geometry families, ε_match shows strong buffer-controlled suppression and is well organized by a two-geometry scaling form. For scaled families, especially a=b=d/8, R_match exhibits a clear crossing and finite-size collapse near p ∼0.09, consistent with a growing recoverability scale near the decoding transition. We use this scaling to formulate an adaptive buffer-selection rule and to identify a distance-scaled initialization for a composite quasi-local RG decoder on the full torus. In the tuned family a₀=b₀=d/8, the resulting logical-failure curves show an apparent finite-size crossing at p≃0.09--0.10, below the conventional MWPM threshold scale. We focus on dephasing noise with perfect syndrome measurements to cleanly isolate the underlying behavior.

item.title: Quantifying the Dual-isotope Advantage for Ytterbium-array Surface Codes using Realistic Noise Models
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Dual-isotope (171Yb-g, 174Yb) surface code with in-place readout achieves lowest logical error rate, where Rydberg-state decay accounts for 74% to 80% of the logical error rate scaling.

Grade 0.396 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit” · Fumiyoshi Kobayashi, Toshi Kusano, Nicholas Fazio, Yuma Nakamura

Figure

Logical error rate per round versus code distance d across various isotope pairings, qubit encodings, and syndrome extraction schemes for rotated and XZZX surface codes.

Asks

How do realistic systemic noise channels affect the surface-code quantum memory performance of dual-isotope ytterbium arrays compared to single-isotope architectures?

But

Simulations using Clifford-compatible twirled noise models; atom-loss detection flags not decoded; specific experimental noise parameters assumed.

Tools

DualYbSim (Stim wrapper) · Generalised Pauli twirling approximation (GPTA) · Rotated and XZZX surface codes · Neutral-atom tweezer arrays (¹⁷¹Yb and ¹⁷⁴Yb)

Abstract

Neutral-atom quantum computers are a promising platform for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but logical performance depends on systemic realistic noise factors during syndrome extraction. In dual-isotope Yb arrays, the roles of data and ancilla qubits are separated spectrally, allowing ancilla qubits to be measured in place without additional transport or shelving operations. Here we quantify the advantage of a dual-isotope Yb architecture for surface code memories. We develop an experimentally motivated Clifford-compatible noise model for dual-isotope 171Yb-174Yb systems using generalised Pauli twirling and implement it as a wrapper for Stim called DualYbSim, which has been packaged as an open source Python library. Simulations of rotated and XZZX surface codes show that a dual-isotope architecture with in-place measurement achieves the lowest logical error rates among the architectures considered, outperforming single-isotope schemes based on shelving or zoned measurement. Our error-budget analysis also identifies Rydberg-state decay as the dominant limitation, contributing to 74-80% of the logical error rate scaling, highlighting concrete experimental targets for improving FTQC performance.

We develop an experimentally motivated Clifford-compatible noise model for dual-isotope 171Yb-174Yb systems using generalised Pauli twirling and implement it as a wrapper for Stim called DualYbSim, which has been packaged as an open source Python library. Simulations of rotated and XZZX surface codes show that a dual-isotope architecture with in-place measurement achieves the lowest logical error rates among the architectures considered, outperforming single-isotope schemes based on shelving or zoned measurement. Our error-budget analysis also identifies Rydberg-state decay as the dominant limitation, contributing to 74-80% of the logical error rate scaling, highlighting concrete experimental targets for improving FTQC performance.

item.title: Quantum Resource Estimation for Simulating the SYK Model with Trotterization, qDRIFT, and Asymmetric Qubitization
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Asymmetric qubitization outperforms Trotterization and qDRIFT in T-gate scaling for SYK simulation, requiring under 5×108 T gates for N=100 Majorana modes at total error εtotal=10−4 (versus >4×109 for qDRIFT), despite needing 159 qubits instead of 50.

Grade 0.378 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Brian Goldsmith, Larissa Kroell, Nishna Aerabati

Figure

Qubit count (top) and total T gates at εtotal=10−4 (bottom) versus number of Majorana modes N for Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization at t=1. Asymmetric qubitization requires more qubits (159 vs 50 at N=100) but yields orders of magnitude fewer T gates.

Asks

What are the concrete qubit and T-gate resource requirements for simulating the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model across Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization algorithms?

But

Theoretical worst-case upper bounds used for PPR method resource scaling; assumed evolution time t=1 and split error equally between algorithm and rotation synthesis (εalg=εrot).

Tools

PsiQuantum Construct (Workbench framework) · Asymmetric qubitization with Quantum Signal Processing · Second-order Trotter-Suzuki decomposition · qDRIFT randomized compilation · Jordan-Wigner transformation

Abstract

The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model has been identified as a promising candidate to run on early fault-tolerant quantum computers due to the relatively modest resources required to probe non-trivial physics (namely holographic duality and AdS/CFT correspondence). As such, it is crucial that the details of how to run such a simulation are well understood. Using PsiQuantum's Construct platform, we implement and analyze three different approaches to simulate the SYK model: Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization with Quantum Signal Processing. We provide an open-source library containing implementations for SYK simulation using all three methods, which we use to obtain quantum resource estimates for qubit and T gate count as functions of the number of Majorana modes and precision. We find that while qDRIFT and Trotterization benefit from a lower qubit count, the large number of T gates required lead to asymmetric qubitization being advantageous in most cases. This reinforces previous theoretical considerations. We intend both the implementations and the estimates to be useful for researchers to continue to study the SYK model and understand how the techniques and resources vary.

item.title: Quantum Fourier transform toolbox
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Explicit quantum Fourier transform circuits scale as poly⁡(log⁡q,log⁡(1/ε)) gates for GL2(𝔽q) and remove the |F|=poly⁡(n) size restriction for wreath products F≀Sn.

Grade 0.367 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “fault-tolerant logical gates and magic state distillation” · Carli Bruinsma, Pietro M. Posta, Joppe Stokvis, Dmitry Grinko, Maris Ozols

Asks

How can efficient non-abelian quantum Fourier transform circuits be systematically constructed for broader classes of finite groups, including finite linear groups and general wreath products?

Before

For finite Lie-type groups of rank k, cost was qO(k) operations (Moore, Rockmore, and Russell); for wreath products H≀Sn, prior generic constructions required |H|=poly⁡(n).

But

Operator-norm precision ε, with gate counts scaling polylogarithmically in 1/ε.

Tools

Mackey theory · Clifford theory · Representation theory of GL₂(F_q) · Subgroup-adapted bases

Abstract

Quantum Fourier transforms (QFTs) are essential primitives in quantum algorithms. While abelian groups admit efficient QFT circuits, with circuit size polynomial in the logarithm of the group order, efficient constructions are known for relatively few non-abelian families. We develop two new approaches to QFT circuit construction, based on Mackey theory and Clifford theory, respectively, and use them to show exponential improvement in circuit cost for specific group families. Using the Mackey-theoretic approach, we obtain explicit quantum circuits for the QFT over GL₂(F_q) that scale polynomially in logq, rather than polynomially in q. Using the Clifford-theoretic approach, we obtain QFT circuits for wreath products FwrS_n, whose cost depends on the cost of a QFT over F and the size of its representation registers. This removes the restriction |F|=poly(n) required by previous generic constructions and can yield exponential improvements when F itself has an efficient QFT. Together, these methods provide new systematic tools to construct QFTs for broad classes of finite groups.
